newsitem.title: CHINA: Copper prices too high, too uncertain for China.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices too high, too uncertain for China.

text.p: Copper prices, having taken a battering in the past couple of trading days, are still too high and too unstable for genuine consumer buying, especially by the cost-conscious Chinese, traders said on Thursday.
"It's still too high for China. There is buying interest but the question is, is the price here for now or will it go lower," a Western trader said.
"The answer is I don't know. I don't think anyone knows where it is going to go," he said.
Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) were driven to their lowest levels in seven weeks on Wednesday, when a wave of speculative selling swept across the floor.
The benchmark three months delivery price fell to $2,355 a tonne at one stage, down $82 from Tuesday.
The beleaguered market is nine percent down from last Friday's $2,594 with last three months business at $2,373 a tonne, still down a hefty $63 from Tuesday's close.
Shanghai copper futures continued the week's falls on Thursday, opening sharply down, with the most actively traded October contract losing 280 yuan to 22,000 yuan ($2,654).
Local support was strong at 21,800 yuan, a Shanghai futures trader said, but he was recommending all his clients sell "because there is no money here for buying".
Traders said despite recent supply tightness, fundamentals were not behind the falls and this made price direction impossible to predict.

"Fundamentals have nothing to do with what is happening at the moment," another trading source said. "While prices were high there were reasons they were high -- physical metal was tight and still is tight for July/August."
Rumours that one user faced huge options-related losses had failed to materialise so far, another trader said.
However, some traders in the region reported that 10,000 tonnes of copper, possibly belonging to LG Metals, was sitting in a South Korean port for shipment to Singapore, where the LME has warehouses.

Some traders said the shipment could be aimed at covering LG Metals' short copper positions on the LME. The company has refused to comment on rumours in London that it faced huge losses on its options positions after the recent rally.
Speculative buying weighed heavy, the Western trader said, amid a belief among consumers, including Chinese end-users, that copper was fundamentally over-priced.

"The Chinese have their levels for different periods both nearby and forward under the market, indicating interest," a trader in Singapore said, adding interest at $1 a lb, or $2,200 a tonne, or under had not changed throughout the rally.

"The end-users feel that in the medium and longer term copper is fundamentally over-valued. With production costs of less than $1,000 a tonne, it can't hold up on a sustained basis at $2,500 or more," he said.

"The good, decent-sized buying interest is still a fair way below the market. But anybody who is short of the market, where do they take profit? How greedy are they? What sort of return are they looking for?" the Singapore trader asked, echoing the prevalent queries.
"They could easily turn this market around $50, $60, $70, pretty quickly too because there are a number of producer hedge sellers trying to work out what's gone on, and why it went on.

"Nothing fundamentally has changed, but they've missed an opportunity to sell and they want to hedge. Do they run in and catch any rally that comes in now or do they wait?" he said. ($1 = 8.3 yuan) -- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
